Optimization and repeated runs

Source: vignettes/articles/optimization.Rmd
optimization.Rmd

smallvis makes it possible to change the objective and optimizer independently. This is useful for experiments, but a setting that works well for t-SNE need not work well for another cost function. Start by changing one choice at a time, keeping preprocessing and initialization fixed.

Configure a method

Use a string for a method’s defaults, or a list whose first element names the method and whose other elements override its options. For example, this configures the balance of repulsion and attraction in the LargeVis cost function:

largevis_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  method = list("largevis", gamma = 1),
  Y_init = "spca",
  perplexity = 30,
  eta = 0.1,
  max_iter = 1000,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(largevis_fit)
## [1] 150   2

The package implements the LargeVis and UMAP cost functions with its own optimization machinery. These runs are different from the original algorithms’ sampled stochastic optimization procedures. The LargeVis and UMAP articles examine those differences; the method-specific options reference lists the available controls.

Change the optimizer

The default is the delta-bar-delta scheme familiar from t-SNE. The opt argument also accepts optimizers provided through mize, with options supplied in a list. For UMAP, t-UMAP, LargeVis, and USNE, function-based line searches require gr_eps = 0 so the gradient matches the objective used by the search:

umap_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  scale = FALSE,
  method = list("umap", gr_eps = 0),
  opt = list("l-bfgs", c1 = 1e-4, c2 = 0.9),
  Y_init = "spca",
  max_iter = 300,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(umap_fit)
## [1] 150   2

Pseudo-separable t-SNE (pstsne) and dynamic HSSNE (dhssne) require a gradient-only optimizer such as Adam or the default delta-bar-delta. The former uses approximate forces; the latter changes alpha between steps, invalidating the objective data retained by function-based optimizers. Use hssne when you want to optimize at a fixed alpha with a line search.

The alternative optimizers reference gives the supported settings. Longer experiments compare L-BFGS, conjugate gradient, spectral directions, and gradient-based adaptive updates.

Use exaggeration

Early exaggeration strengthens attractive interactions for an initial phase. In this t-SNE run, input probabilities are multiplied by 4 for the first 100 iterations:

exaggerated_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  Y_init = "spca",
  perplexity = 30,
  eta = 100,
  exaggeration_factor = 4,
  stop_lying_iter = 100,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

late_exaggeration_factor and start_late_lying_iter enable a later phase; the late exaggeration experiments explore its effect. Function-based line searches are restricted to configurations whose objective and gradient agree; smallvis reports unsupported combinations rather than silently treating them as ordinary optimization.

Compare random starts

smallvis_rep() runs from random initial coordinates and returns the result with the lowest final cost. It overrides Y_init; built-in methods share one prepared input graph across the starts. With ret_extra = TRUE, all_costs contains the final cost from each run:

set.seed(42)
best <- smallvis_rep(
  nrep = 3,
  X = iris,
  perplexity = 30,
  ret_extra = TRUE,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
best$all_costs
## [1] 0.1257062 0.1293343 0.1258536
sum(best$costs)
## [1] 0.1257062

This comparison holds the objective and affinities fixed. Costs from different methods or input graphs generally have different meanings and should not be used as a universal embedding score. Use keep_all = TRUE to inspect every layout; see the repeated-run reference.

Step down through perplexities

smallvis_perpstep() starts with larger perplexities, then optimizes at the requested target. The step_iter budget is taken out of max_iter, rather than added to it:

stepped_fit <- smallvis_perpstep(
  X = iris,
  Y_init = "spca",
  perplexity = 30,
  step_iter = 50,
  max_iter = 300,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(stepped_fit)
## [1] 150   2

The perplexity-stepping reference describes the schedule and which controls apply to the final phase.
